summary.traveler: Travellers entering or leaving Brazil carrying BRL 10,000 or more (approximately USD 2,000) in Brazilian reais, or the equivalent in foreign currency or monetary instruments, must declare this to the Receita Federal (Brazilian Federal Revenue Service) at customs. There is no restriction on the amount that may be carried; only the declaration obligation applies. The Brazilian real is subject to a managed float administered by the Banco Central do Brasil (BCB).
summary.business: Brazil maintains a partially liberalised foreign exchange regime under Resolution CMN 3.568 and subsequent Banco Central regulations. Current account transactions are broadly liberalised. Capital account transactions — including FDI, portfolio investment, and financial derivatives — require registration with the Banco Central do Brasil electronic system (SISBACEN/ROF). Brazilian residents face limits on keeping funds abroad without BCB registration. Businesses must comply with Brazilian AML law under Law 9.613/1998.

rules.bring_foreign_currency_in: Travellers entering Brazil may bring any amount of foreign currency or Brazilian reais. However, amounts of BRL 10,000 or more (or the equivalent in foreign currency or monetary instruments) must be declared to the Receita Federal at the port of entry on Form e-DBV (Declaração de Porte de Valores) or the electronic equivalent. Failure to declare constitutes a customs violation under Brazilian law and may result in confiscation and administrative penalties.
rules.take_foreign_currency_out: Travellers leaving Brazil may take out any amount of currency but must declare amounts of BRL 10,000 or more (or foreign currency equivalent) to the Receita Federal at departure. Foreign currency purchases for international travel must be made through authorised financial institutions. Brazilian residents leaving permanently or semi-permanently must comply with BCB regulations on the maintenance of funds abroad, including registration requirements for deposits in foreign financial institutions.
rules.cash_declaration_threshold: The declaration threshold in Brazil is BRL 10,000 or its foreign currency equivalent. Travellers carrying cash, travellers cheques, or pre-paid cards above this amount must complete the Currency Carry-on Electronic Declaration (Declaracao Eletronica de Porte de Valores - E-DPV) issued by the Brazilian Federal Revenue Service (Receita Federal) at receita.fazenda.gov.br/dpv. This applies at both arrival and departure. The BCB confirms that there is no limit on the amount of cash travellers may carry, but amounts above BRL 10,000 must be declared. For domestic exchange transactions above BRL 10,000 in cash, payment must be made by bank transfer or cheque rather than cash. Failure to declare amounts above the threshold may result in confiscation and criminal sanctions under Brazilian law. BCB Resolution No. 277 of December 31, 2022 governs foreign exchange operations. Source: bcb.gov.br/dinheirobrasileiro/en/informacoes-sobre-cambio.html.
rules.resident_holding_rules: Brazilian residents are permitted to hold foreign currency accounts abroad but must register these with the Banco Central do Brasil (BCB) through the designated electronic reporting system when balances exceed USD 1,000. Annual reporting to the BCB (Declaração de Capitais Brasileiros no Exterior — CBE) is required for residents with foreign assets above USD 1,000,000 as of 31 December each year. Quarterly reporting applies for residents with foreign assets above USD 100,000,000. Residents may purchase foreign currency for authorised purposes through BCB-licensed financial institutions.
rules.non_resident_rules: Non-residents may hold foreign currency accounts in Brazil through BCB-authorised banks. Foreign capital entering Brazil — for investment, loans, or other purposes — must be registered with the BCB through the ROF (Registro de Operações Financeiras) system. Registered foreign capital may be repatriated, including returns and profits, subject to documentation and BCB compliance. Non-registered foreign capital faces restrictions on repatriation.
rules.business_invoicing_settlement: Brazilian businesses must conduct foreign exchange transactions through BCB-authorised financial institutions. All FX transactions are reported to the BCB through the electronic SISBACEN system. Export proceeds must generally be received in foreign currency and converted to BRL through an authorised bank within 360 days of shipment. Foreign direct investment and external loans must be registered with the BCB. Businesses may maintain foreign currency accounts abroad for operational purposes subject to BCB registration requirements.
rules.exchange_controls: Brazil maintains a partially liberalised foreign exchange regime. The Brazilian real operates under a managed float. Current account transactions (trade, services, transfers) are broadly liberalised. Capital account transactions require BCB registration. The Banco Central do Brasil may intervene in the FX market through spot sales, swaps, and repurchase operations to manage exchange rate volatility. Inflows and outflows of foreign capital are tracked through the BCB's electronic registration systems. AML compliance is required under Law 9.613/1998.
rules.banking_conversion_practicality: Foreign currency exchange is available through BCB-authorised banks and licensed exchange dealers. ATMs accepting international cards are broadly available in major cities. Exchange rates for the BRL/USD and BRL/EUR are published daily by the BCB (PTAX rate). Large currency exchange transactions require identity documentation and are subject to BCB reporting. The Brazilian Payments System (SPB) facilitates interbank settlements. International transfers are processed via SWIFT through BCB-authorised institutions.

disclaimer: This page provides general informational reference only. Brazil's foreign exchange rules are complex and subject to frequent regulatory updates by the Banco Central do Brasil. CBE reporting requirements and ROF registration obligations for foreign capital are separate legal requirements. This is not legal, regulatory, tax, financial, or compliance advice. Always verify current rules with the BCB, Receita Federal, or a qualified Brazilian legal or compliance professional before making any financial or travel decisions.
